# **Employers Plan More Hiring and Fewer Pay Raises in the Year Ahead**


## **The 2026 ZipRecruiter Employer Report**


### **Key takeaways**


-


**Hiring momentum builds:** 67% of employers expect to increase hiring over the next year (up from 63% in 2025), and 61% are already expanding headcount, compared to just 50% last year.


-


**But employers aren’t all in on pay raises:** 59% of employers plan to increase pay over the next year, down from 61% in 2025 and 79% in 2024.


-


**Workers have stayed put this year:** Employers reported lower turnover in 2026.


-


**AI optimism drives hiring plans:** AI is now driving headcount growth across multiple industries, and 41% of employers are paying a wage premium for AI skills.


-


**Entry-level hiring rebounds:** 36% of employers plan to make entry-level talent a larger share of their hires, up from 32% last year, while just 11% plan to shrink it, down from 14%.


-


**Employers are working harder to verify candidates:** 55% have added ID or background checks, 53% require live or in-person skills tests, and 30% use AI-detection software. Only 15% have taken no steps.


-


**Critical thinking tops the skills gap:** Critical thinking is now the skill employers say candidates lack most (44%), and in the Information sector, the share rises to 62%.


> “
>
>
> For employers who are looking to maintain stability where they can, the low turnover environment is providing a key opportunity to invest in their existing workforces. But today’s low turnover largely reflects market dynamics, and our surveys show that workers are already planning their next move. Zooming in on the most important factors facing workers, like compensation and benefits and the rollout of AI within the org, is essential for the long run. ”


— Nicole Bachaud, ZipRecruiter Labor Economist


### **The labor market is caught in a stalemate as workers hold their cards**


The labor market still appears locked in place. Last year, we predicted 2026 would bring a gradual reacceleration in hiring after most employers reported plans to grow headcount throughout the year. Hiring improved from 2025’s slump, but ongoing headwinds and a shrinking labor pool keep job growth soft compared to historic trends.


As of the end of 2026, workers are holding their cards and prioritizing stability. Employee turnover fell to a median of 15% in 2026, down from 49% the year before.


Low turnover suggests limited mobility, but employers are taking advantage of current worker stickiness as retention remains their top priority. In 2026, 72% of employers put internal stability as their top priority—retention (38%) and upskilling (34%)—down only slightly from 76% in 2025. What keeps employees happily in place is a different mix of tools than it was even a year ago. While workplace culture remains foundational, employers in 2026 named competitive pay (66%) and comprehensive benefits (55%) as their strongest retention tools.


Some employers are boosting benefit offerings as more workers zoom in on benefit packages. On ZipRecruiter, 54% of job postings mention benefits, up from 53% a year ago and trending up over time.


For companies with lower turnover in 2026, compensation is now identified as one of the top reasons workers stay. And for companies with higher turnover, inadequate compensation was the top reason why in 2026.

DDespite identifying compensation as their primary retention tool, employers are pulling back on future salary growth. **In 2026, 59% of employers plan to increase pay, down from 61% in 2025 and a material drop from 79% in 2024.** Many workers see[higher pay when they move jobs](https://www.atlantafed.org/research-and-data/data/wage-growth-tracker) . With limited turnover and mobility in this market and fewer planned pay bumps, higher pay is looking harder to achieve, adding financial pressure to job seekers as many already find themselves[financially strapped](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/job-seeker-confidence-2026-q3#:~:text=The%20drop%20in%20confidence%20from%20job%20seekers%20isn%E2%80%99t%20only%20stemming%20from%20the%20labor%20market%3B%20many%20are%20facing%20greater%20financial%20challenges%20than%20earlier%20this%20year.) .


The low-turnover environment might suggest employers can afford to dial back on pay increases, but doing so could create hidden vulnerabilities. While workers appear locked in place today, many are already quietly eyeing the exit. In fact,[a quarter of workers are planning their next move based on how their current workplace uses AI](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/2026-ai-worker-report#:~:text=AI%20might%20lead%20to%20the%20next%20wave%20of%20worker%20turnover) , making comprehensive compensation strategies vital to keeping a stable workforce once the market unlocks.

### **AI emerges as the wildcard for headcount growth**


When asked about forward-looking plans, over two-thirds of employers (67%) expect to increase hiring over the next year—an increase from 63% in the 2025 survey. And many aren’t waiting: 61% report that they are already actively expanding headcount, up from 50% last year, primarily driven by rising customer demand (cited by 78% of expanding employers).


Looking ahead, hiring intentions are ramping up for two specific categories:


-


**Full-time workers:** 91% are hiring full-time roles, up from 87% in 2025.


-


**Entry-level talent:** 36% of employers are planning to make entry-level talent a larger share of overall hires (an increase from 32% last year), while only 11% plan to make entry-level talent a smaller share of overall hires (down from 14% last year).


The increased focus on full-time and entry-level roles is welcome news to young job seekers, as[AI threatens to block opportunities to gain work experience](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/ai-employer-report-2026#:~:text=Entry%2Dlevel%20roles%20are%20having%20a%20rougher%20time%20despite%20an%20otherwise%20bright%20hiring%20picture%3A%2038%25%20of%20employers%20have%20shifted%20basic%20data%20processing%20away%20from%20entry%2Dlevel%20workers%20and%20onto%20AI%2C%20and%2031%25%20have%20raised%20experience%20requirements%20for%20entry%2Dlevel%20jobs%20as%20a%20result.) . But without intentional on-ramps to[prepare young workers for these entry-level roles](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/2026-ai-worker-report#:~:text=Trickle%2Ddown%20training%20doesn%E2%80%99t%20land) (which[31% of employers say they are raising the experience bar for](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/ai-employer-report-2026#:~:text=and%2031%25%20have%20raised%20experience%20requirements%20for%20entry%2Dlevel%20jobs%20as%20a%20result.) ), many young workers may still be shut out of these hiring plans.

As hiring plans loom for most employers, many are pointing to AI as a source of growth, with 30% expecting AI to increase headcount, up from 19% last year. Additionally, the share of employers saying AI will decrease headcount dropped from 26% to 21%, further solidifying the newfound optimism employers see in AI’s potential. In[2025, the Tech/Information industry was alone in saying AI would add headcount, vs. reduce it.](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/employer-survey-2025#:~:text=Telecommunications%2C%20Technology%2C%20Internet%20%26%20Electronics%2C%20Advertising%20%26%20Marketing%2C%20and%20Professional%20and%20Business%20Services%20employers%20see%20the%20biggest%20upside%2C%20with%20the%20share%20of%20employers%20anticipating%20an%20increase%20in%20headcount%20due%20to%20AI%20at%2037.7%25%2C%2030.0%25%2C%20and%2024.4%25%2C%20respectively.) In 2026, AI optimism has swept through the broader labor market, fundamentally changing how industries plan to grow.


More employers are paying a premium to acquire these skills. **Across the board, 41% of employers now pay a wage premium for AI talent.** Unsurprisingly, the industries heavily banking on AI for headcount growth are paying the most aggressively:

While AI is seen as an overall headcount driver, massive restructuring is happening beneath the surface. Of employers that conducted recent layoffs, 23% cite AI and automation as a primary reason, still below the top two reasons: cost-cutting (34%) and restructuring (33%). **Notably, the employers most optimistic about AI-driven headcount growth are also those most likely to attribute workforce reductions to AI** , signaling that restructuring is underway, even as some jobs grow.


Among employers that conducted layoffs, the sectors most likely to cite AI and automation as a factor are:


-


Information/Tech (44%)


-


Financial Activities (35%)


-


Professional and Business Services (31%)


As employers adjust the skills they need, they are replacing older roles with new, AI-ready positions. **On ZipRecruiter, 7.4% of jobs in October were AI-related** , up from 4% last October, as roles continue to evolve across the market.


### **Employers raise the stakes to shuffle through the rise in applications**


Workers aren’t the only ones watching AI closely. Job seekers are using tools and resources to help them apply for their next role. While[AI-assisted job seekers are twice as likely to land a role](https://www.ziprecruiter-research.org/economic-insights-research/ai-powered-job-seekers) , AI assistance is also leading to far more applications overall. **Employers now sift through a median of 50 applications per open position, up significantly from the 35 seen in 2025.**

So far, this increase in applications has not extended hiring timelines, as employers leverage AI themselves to streamline their processes. In fact, the median time to fill an open role dropped from 26 days in 2025 to just 20 days in 2026—saving employers nearly a week per role despite higher application volumes.


With AI making polished applications easy to produce, employers are working harder to confirm candidates are who they say they are. Over half (55%) added ID or background checks, 53% require live or in-person skills tests, and 30% use AI-detection software, while only 15% have taken no measures.


Employers also use the application requirements as another way to sense candidate quality and intent. Two in three employers (66%) require three or more application components, and one in three employers (34%) require four or more. To filter candidates, employers require:

While overall hiring timelines have improved, adding more steps to the application and hiring process does slow things down. Roles requiring one application component (i.e., just a resume or application form) take a median of 14 days to fill. Roles requiring four components stretch to 21 days, and roles requiring seven materials drag out to a median of 26 days.


These extra steps strain employers’ own HR and recruiting staff. Among employers requiring four components, 14% say a lack of time or bandwidth is keeping them from making hires, more than double the 5.7% among employers requiring just one component.


Adding more steps to the hiring process might also be screening out too many candidates too early. Employers who rank a "lack of quality candidates" as their top recruitment challenge require slightly more application components on average, suggesting that overly tedious processes may exclude top talent too early.


### **Changing the rules: Human skills remain the tiebreaker**


With AI tools making it easier than ever for job seekers to submit perfectly polished applications, the sheer volume of resumes makes it difficult for true matches to stand out. To cut through the noise, employers are changing the rules of the game—moving away from resume-only screening and leaning into testing that asks candidates to show what they can do right up front. Even in a highly digitized labor market, foundational human skills remain the ultimate tiebreaker.


When evaluating candidates, the specific traits employers struggle to find are almost entirely soft skills.

In the most AI-exposed industries, these human skills are more vital than ever. In the Information sector, a massive 62% of employers cite a lack of critical thinking in their candidates; the top missing skill is exactly what’s needed to evaluate and judge AI outputs, meaning roles that used to be more technical are now more focused on soft skills.


Because resumes alone make authentic soft skills hard to gauge, employers are adapting their screening strategies. **Skill tests are now part of the process for 48% of employers, up from 38% last year.** Four in ten employers (40%) who require a skill test still rank a 'lack of quality candidates' as their top recruitment challenge, compared to 36% of employers who don't use assessments. Rather than serving as a hurdle, skill assessments give candidates a meaningful platform to highlight their practical abilities as traditional resumes become more standardized.


### **In summary**


Today’s low turnover largely reflects market conditions, not that employers have fully solved retention. As hiring picks up and workers regain leverage, the gaps this report highlights will matter more: pay that isn’t keeping up with expectations, skills employers want but aren’t training for, and hiring processes slowed by extra steps. Employers that address these now, while the market is quieter, will be better positioned to retain their people and compete for new ones in 2027.


### **Methodology**


ZipRecruiter conducted a national online survey between September 8 and 16, 2026, to explore employer attitudes toward recent hiring trends and their experiences of current U.S. labor market conditions. The survey was administered to a PureSpectrum panel of 1,500+ verified talent acquisition professionals and hiring managers, each with considerable responsibility for hiring processes and decisions. They were drawn from businesses of various sizes across a wide range of industries. In addition to standard screening and demographic questions, respondents were asked about their recruiting, hiring, employment, and retention practices, as well as their expectations, desires, and requirements for future talent acquisition activities.
